title: Find the Merge Point of Two Linked Lists
directAnswer: Two pointers, one per list. When a pointer hits the end, redirect it to the *other* list's head. After at most one switch each, both pointers have walked lenA + lenB nodes and meet exactly at the intersection node — or both reach null together if the lists never merge. O(n + m) time, O(1) space, no length math needed.

remember.pattern: Switching-heads two pointers (equalize path lengths by swapping lists)
remember.formula:
a, b = headA, headB
while a is not b:
    a = a.next if a else headB
    b = b.next if b else headA
return a   # the intersection node, or null
rules: Compare nodes by **identity** (`a == b` / `a is b`), never by value — two equal values aren't the same node.
When a pointer hits null, redirect it to the **other** list's head — not its own — to cancel the length difference.
Redirect to the head on the step *after* reaching null, so each pointer walks exactly lenA + lenB and they align.
If the lists don't intersect, both pointers become null on the same step and `a is b` (both null) ends the loop → return null.
Do **not** mutate the lists; this is a read-only traversal (no cycles are created).
whenToUse: Find where two singly linked lists join into a shared tail (Y-shape)
Detect a shared suffix without knowing the lengths in advance
Any 'two paths converge' problem on pointer-based structures
When O(1) extra space is required and you can't use a hash set
antiSignals: The lists may form a cycle → handle the cycle first (Floyd), this assumes acyclic Y-shape
You can mutate freely and want the simplest code → a hash set of one list's nodes is more obvious
You only need whether they intersect, not the node → still works, but a set answers it too
Nodes can be compared by value uniquely → still compare by reference; values may repeat
remember.takeaway: The switching-heads trick equalizes two unequal path lengths without ever measuring them: after each pointer crosses into the other list, both have lenA + lenB to walk, so they land on the join together. It's the cleanest O(1)-space answer and the same length-alignment idea behind many two-pointer problems.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you compare nodes by reference rather than value, and whether you can equalize two different list lengths — either by switching heads or by advancing the longer list first — without brute-forcing all pairs.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Comparing a.val == b.val instead of a == b (a node identity), or building the length-difference solution off-by-one so the pointers never align.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Lead with the switching-heads two-pointer for O(1) space, explain *why* both pointers walk lenA + lenB, and mention the hash-set and length-difference alternatives as trade-offs.

problemStatement:
You are given the heads of two singly linked lists, `headA` and `headB`. The two lists may **merge** at some node — after which they share all subsequent nodes (a Y-shape).

Return *the node at which the two lists intersect*. If they do not intersect, return `null`.

Intersection is by node **identity**, not value. The lists are acyclic and must not be modified.
constraints: If the lists intersect, they share a common suffix (no diverging after the merge)
The lists are acyclic; do not modify them
understanding: If two singly linked lists merge, they can never split again — once they share a node they share every node after it (each node has exactly one next). So the intersection is the first shared node. The challenge is the lists can have different lengths before the join, so naive aligned walking from both heads misses it.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is intersection defined by node identity or by equal values?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: By identity — the same physical node. Two different nodes with the same value are not an intersection, so I compare references, not vals.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can the two lists have different lengths before merging?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes — that's the whole difficulty. The pre-merge tails can differ in length, so I need to cancel that difference before comparing.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Am I allowed to modify the lists?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No. I'll only read next pointers; I won't reverse, splice, or add cycles.

clarifyingQuestions.question: What if one or both lists are empty?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: If either head is null there can be no intersection, so the answer is null — and the algorithms handle it naturally.

diagrams.title: Picking the right approach
diagrams.caption: Switching-heads gives O(1) space with no length math; a hash set is simplest to reason about but O(n) space.

approaches.name: Hash Set — Remember One List's Nodes (Baseline)
approaches.whenToMention: Say this first as the obvious, easy-to-verify answer, then improve the space with the two-pointer trick.
hints: If you wrote down every node of list A, how would you then test each node of list B?
Store node references (not values) in a hash set as you walk A.
Walk B and return the first node already in the set — that's the first shared node, the intersection.
approaches.complexityReasoning: One pass over A to fill the set (n inserts), one pass over B to probe (m lookups), each O(1) average → O(n + m) time. The set holds up to n node references → O(n) space.
approaches.explanation:
We record the identity of every node in one list, then scan the other for the first match.

**Why store nodes, not values.** Intersection is defined by identity, so the set must hold node *references*. If we stored values, two distinct nodes holding the same number would falsely register as a merge. In Java that's an `IdentityHashMap`-style set or just a `HashSet<ListNode>` (default identity hashCode); in Python, object `id` semantics make `set()` of nodes do the right thing.

**Why the first hit in B is the answer.** Because a singly linked list can't split, the moment list B steps onto a node that belongs to A, every following node is shared too. So the *first* node of B found in the set is precisely the merge point.

**Why we still want better.** This is correct and trivially explainable, but it costs O(n) memory. Interviewers usually push for O(1) space, which the two-pointer switch achieves. Lead with this to show the idea, then optimize.
approaches.insight: Membership testing turns 'do these paths share a node?' into 'have I seen this exact node before?' — the same remember-and-probe shape as Two Sum, applied to references instead of values.

approaches.name: Two Pointers — Switch Heads at the End (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The O(1)-space answer interviewers want. Phrase it as 'cancel the length difference by swapping lists', not just 'two pointers'.
hints: The only thing stopping a simple side-by-side walk is that the two lists have different lengths before the join. How could you make both pointers travel the *same* total distance?
Let each pointer, on reaching the end of its list, jump to the head of the OTHER list. How far has each pointer traveled when they meet?
After the switch, pointer A walks lenA + lenB and pointer B walks lenB + lenA — equal totals — so they arrive at the intersection on the same step. If there's no intersection, they hit null together.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Each pointer traverses at most lenA + lenB nodes before meeting or both reaching null → O(n + m) time. Only two pointers are used → O(1) space.
approaches.explanation:
We run one pointer down each list; whenever a pointer runs off the end, we send it to the *other* list's head. After the swap the pointers are length-aligned and meet at the join.

**The length problem, and the fix.** If list A is shorter, a pointer at A's head and one at B's head are misaligned: when both step together, A's pointer reaches the shared tail 'too early'. The switch fixes this without measuring anything. Pointer `a` walks `lenA`, then crosses to B and walks `lenB_before_merge` to reach the join — total `lenA + (lenB_before)`. Pointer `b` walks `lenB`, crosses to A, walks `lenA_before` — total `lenB + (lenA_before)`. Since `lenA = lenA_before + shared` and `lenB = lenB_before + shared`, both totals equal `lenA_before + lenB_before + shared` = `lenA + lenB_before` = `lenB + lenA_before`. Equal distances → they land on the intersection together.

**Compare by identity.** The loop condition is `a != b` comparing node *references*. When they point at the same physical node, that node is the merge point. Never compare `a.val == b.val` — distinct nodes can share a value.

**Why the no-intersection case terminates.** If the lists never merge, each pointer walks `lenA + lenB` and then becomes null. Crucially, both become null on the *same* step (they've each traveled `lenA + lenB`), so `a == b` holds with both being null and the loop exits returning null — no infinite loop.

**Why redirect on the step after null, not skip null.** The trick relies on each pointer 'spending' exactly one step at the boundary. Reading `a = a.next if a else headB` means when `a` is null we send it to `headB`; the symmetric null arrivals are what guarantee the equal-distance meeting (including the both-null exit).
approaches.insight: Switching heads is a way to make two unequal lengths equal *for free* — no counting, no second pass to measure. The named trap is comparing values instead of node identity; the second trap is sending a null pointer back to its own head instead of the other's, which breaks the length cancellation.

pitfalls: Comparing a.val == b.val instead of node identity — false matches on repeated values.
On reaching null, jumping to the SAME list's head instead of the other — the length difference never cancels and you loop forever.
Skipping null instead of spending one step on it — breaks the equal-distance guarantee, including the both-null exit.
Assuming the lists are cyclic — this method requires acyclic lists; detect/remove cycles first.

commonMistakes: Comparing node values rather than node identity to decide intersection.
Redirecting a finished pointer to its own head instead of the other list's head.
Computing the length difference with an off-by-one so the aligned walk misses the join.
Assuming both lists are the same length and walking side by side without alignment.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Comparing values instead of identity
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Intersection means the same physical node. Two different nodes can hold equal values (e.g. both 8), so a value comparison reports a false merge before the real one.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Switching to the wrong head
commonMistakesDetailed.why: The length cancellation only works if a finished pointer crosses into the OTHER list. Sending it back to its own head keeps the same length and the pointers never align — an infinite loop on intersecting lists.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
a = headA if a is None else a.next   # wrong: back to own head
b = headB if b is None else b.next
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
a = headB if a is None else a.next   # cross to the other list
b = headA if b is None else b.next

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Off-by-one in the length-difference method
commonMistakesDetailed.why: An alternative is to advance the longer list by |lenA − lenB| first, then walk together. Miscounting the difference (or which list is longer) shifts the alignment so the pointers pass the intersection without meeting.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
diff = lenA - lenB
for _ in range(diff):   # negative when B is longer → no-op, misaligned
    a = a.next
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
diff = abs(lenA - lenB)
longer = a if lenA > lenB else b
for _ in range(diff):
    longer = longer.next
